name: Algorithm Design and Analysis
description: Designing algorithms rather than recalling them: divide and conquer, greedy methods, dynamic programming, advanced graph algorithms, amortised analysis and an introduction to intractability.

topics.name: Divide and Conquer
topics.summary: Splitting a problem into independent subproblems, and the recurrences that describe the cost.

subtopics.name: Solving Recurrences
subtopics.summary: Recursion trees, substitution and the master theorem.

objectives.text: Write the recurrence describing a divide-and-conquer algorithm
Apply the master theorem to solve a recurrence of standard form
Solve a recurrence by the substitution method and verify the bound

subtopics.name: Classic Divide-and-Conquer Algorithms
subtopics.summary: Binary search, merge sort, closest pair and fast integer multiplication.

objectives.text: Explain how Karatsuba multiplication beats the schoolbook method asymptotically
Describe the divide-and-conquer solution to the closest pair problem
Identify when a problem decomposes into independent subproblems

subtopics.name: Order Statistics and Selection
subtopics.summary: Finding the kth smallest element in linear expected time.

objectives.text: Describe quickselect and state its expected and worst-case complexity
Explain how median-of-medians guarantees linear worst-case selection
Compare selection by sorting with direct selection

topics.name: Greedy Algorithms
topics.summary: Taking the locally best option — and proving that it is globally optimal.

subtopics.name: The Greedy Choice Property
subtopics.summary: When a locally optimal choice leads to a global optimum, and how to prove it.

objectives.text: State the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure
Prove a greedy algorithm correct by an exchange argument
Give a problem where the obvious greedy strategy fails

subtopics.name: Scheduling and Huffman Coding
subtopics.summary: Interval scheduling, activity selection and optimal prefix codes.

objectives.text: Solve an interval scheduling problem with the correct greedy criterion
Construct a Huffman code for a given set of frequencies
Explain why Huffman coding produces an optimal prefix code

subtopics.name: Minimum Spanning Trees
subtopics.summary: Kruskal and Prim, the cut property, and union-find.

objectives.text: Trace Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms on a weighted graph
State the cut property and use it to justify correctness
Explain how union-find supports Kruskal's algorithm efficiently

topics.name: Dynamic Programming
topics.summary: Overlapping subproblems solved once and reused — the most powerful design technique in the course.

subtopics.name: Overlapping Subproblems and Memoisation
subtopics.summary: Top-down memoisation and bottom-up tabulation of the same recurrence.

objectives.text: Identify overlapping subproblems in a naive recursion
Convert a recursive solution to a memoised one and state the complexity gain
Rewrite a memoised solution as a bottom-up table

subtopics.name: Dynamic Programming on Sequences
subtopics.summary: Longest common subsequence, edit distance and the knapsack problem.

objectives.text: Formulate the recurrence for edit distance and fill its table
Solve a 0/1 knapsack instance by dynamic programming
Reconstruct an optimal solution from a completed DP table

subtopics.name: Designing a Dynamic Program
subtopics.summary: Choosing the state, the transition and the evaluation order.

objectives.text: Define the DP state and transition for an unfamiliar problem
Determine a valid evaluation order from the dependency structure
Analyse the time and space complexity of a DP formulation

topics.name: Advanced Graph Algorithms
topics.summary: Beyond traversal — shortest paths with negative weights, flows and connectivity.

objectives.text: Apply Bellman-Ford and explain how it detects a negative cycle
Compute all-pairs shortest paths with Floyd-Warshall
Choose the appropriate shortest-path algorithm for stated graph properties

subtopics.name: Network Flow
subtopics.summary: Max-flow, residual graphs, Ford-Fulkerson and the max-flow min-cut theorem.

objectives.text: Compute a maximum flow using augmenting paths on a residual graph
State the max-flow min-cut theorem and identify a minimum cut
Model a matching or assignment problem as a flow network

subtopics.name: Connectivity and Topological Order
subtopics.summary: Strongly connected components, topological sorting and DAG shortest paths.

objectives.text: Produce a topological ordering of a directed acyclic graph
Identify strongly connected components of a directed graph
Exploit a topological order to solve DAG shortest paths in linear time

topics.name: Amortised Analysis
topics.summary: Averaging cost over a sequence of operations rather than bounding the worst single one.

subtopics.name: Aggregate, Accounting and Potential Methods
subtopics.summary: Three techniques for bounding the cost of an operation sequence.

objectives.text: Apply the aggregate method to bound a sequence of operations
Use the accounting method with a credit invariant
Define a potential function and use it to derive an amortised bound

subtopics.name: Disjoint Sets
subtopics.summary: Union by rank, path compression and near-constant amortised cost.

objectives.text: Implement union-find with union by rank and path compression
Explain why path compression improves amortised performance
Trace the structure produced by a sequence of union and find operations

subtopics.name: Amortised Data Structures
subtopics.summary: Dynamic arrays, multipop stacks and binary counters.

objectives.text: Prove the amortised O(1) cost of dynamic array append
Analyse the cost of incrementing a binary counter over many operations
Distinguish amortised cost from average-case cost

topics.name: Intractability
topics.summary: Problems for which no efficient algorithm is known, and how to recognise one.

subtopics.name: P, NP and Verification
subtopics.summary: Decision problems, polynomial time, certificates and the P versus NP question.

objectives.text: Define the classes P and NP in terms of solving and verifying
Give a certificate for a problem in NP and describe its verification
State the P versus NP question and its significance

subtopics.name: NP-Completeness and Reductions
subtopics.summary: Polynomial-time reduction, NP-hardness and the standard complete problems.

objectives.text: Explain what a polynomial-time reduction establishes
Show a problem is NP-complete given a reduction from a known NP-complete problem
Name several standard NP-complete problems

subtopics.name: Coping with Intractability
subtopics.summary: Approximation, heuristics and exploiting special structure.

objectives.text: Describe an approximation algorithm and state its approximation ratio
Explain how restricting the input can make a hard problem tractable
Choose a practical strategy for an NP-hard problem in a stated setting

sources.title: International undergraduate consensus core (MIT, Cambridge, Imperial, Berkeley)
